query: Consider the following context: Melting properties are critical for designing novel materials, especially for discovering high-performance, high-melting refractory materials. Experimental measurements of these properties are extremely challenging due to their high melting temperatures. Complementary theoretical predictions are, therefore, indispensable. One of the most accurate approaches for this purpose is the ab initio free-energy approach based on density functional theory (DFT). However, it generally involves expensive thermodynamic integration using ab initio molecular dynamic simulations. The high computational cost makes high-throughput calculations infeasible. In that context, which method can be used for calculate its melting properties, including the melting temperature, entropy and enthalpy of fusion, and volume change at the melting point, and why?

generation.hypothesis: We hypothesize that the direct solid–liquid coexistence (two-phase) simulation method, applied with suitably accurate classical or machine-learned interatomic potentials, can be used to obtain reliable melting temperatures, enthalpies and entropies of fusion, and volume changes at the melting point with substantially reduced computational cost compared to full ab initio thermodynamic integration.
generation.material_initial_state: A generic high-melting metal or compound with an existing parameterization or training set for a classical or machine-learned potential
generation.intervention: Use direct solid–liquid coexistence simulations under molecular dynamics with an affordable interatomic potential instead of full ab initio free-energy methods
generation.conditions: Establish an initial simulation cell containing both solid and liquid phases in contact at a selected temperature range under constant pressure to allow observation of the equilibrium interface and phase stability
generation.structural_mediator: Application of classical or machine-learned interatomic potentials to represent the respective solid and liquid atomic configurations consistently
generation.mechanism: Through direct simulation of the coexisting phases, the method gives the equilibrium melting temperature and allows calculation of the enthalpy, entropy, and volume changes associated with the solid–liquid transition without requiring expensive thermodynamic integration purely at the DFT level
generation.predicted_outcome: Accurate determination of melting temperature, entropy and enthalpy of fusion, and volume change at melting for high-temperature materials at lower computational cost relative to full ab initio simulations
generation.baseline: Ab initio free-energy integration results from density functional theory molecular dynamics
generation.boundary: This approach depends on the reliability of the chosen interatomic potential or machine-learned model; lack of sufficient training data or inaccurate force fields may degrade predictive accuracy
generation.uncertainty: The exact accuracy of such simulations relative to experiment or ab initio data remains to be quantified and may depend on the quality of the adopted potential

falsification_experiment.design: Perform direct coexistence MD simulations for a known refractory metal or ceramic using both (1) an interatomic potential, and (2) ab initio thermodynamic integration; compare the resulting melting temperature, enthalpy of fusion, entropy of fusion, and volume change from both approaches against reliable experimental data when available
measurements: Equilibrium melting temperature determined via the stationary position of the solid–liquid interface
Enthalpy of fusion via internal energy differences between solid and liquid
Entropy of fusion by dividing enthalpy of fusion by the melting temperature
Volume change by measuring average volumes of the coexisting solid and liquid
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the direct coexistence method using a given potential yields melting properties that systematically deviate from reference ab initio or experimental values (e.g., by more than 5%), the hypothesis that it is a reliable, lower-cost alternative is refuted for that system.
